newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Gulf Coast gasoline firms, driven by traders.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Gulf Coast gasoline firms, driven by traders.

text.p: Gasoline prices in the volatile U.S. Gulf Coast gasoline market headed higher early Friday, with the move dominated by traders rather than refiners, market players said.
"Gas has just exploded," said one trader who said prompt "M1" regular 87-octane unleaded gasoline was changing hands at 2.00 cents over August NYMEX unleaded.
August futures hit a high of 59.90 cents/gallon during the morning but eased back to 59.40 cents by 1119 EDT/1519 GMT, up 0.80 cent on the day.
"There is nothing that is startlingly bullish in the most recent numbers; inventories and production are still high," said Pat Hughes, an analyst at Chevron Corp.

But he added it is the traditional time of year when refiners can run into trouble. As refineries run at full capacity, they are prone to accidents which can curtail prodoction and a fire halting production at Mobil Corp's hydrocracker at Chalmette, Louisiana this week might have given the market a "psychological" boost.
"I don't see anything structurally different in gasoline," said Tom Bentz, an energy market analyst at High Yield Analytics.
"It seems like a short-term phenomenon ahead of some pipeline scheduling and maybe some buying ahead of Tosco, Bayway's maintenance at the end of the month," Bentz added.
Tosco's Bayway refinery is one of the largest in the country and the dominant gasoline supplier on the East Coast.
Volatility often increases ahead of the Houston-to-New York Colonial Pipeline scheduling deadline for shipment on Colonial's now prompt back 20th scheduling cycle, traders said.

Traders appeared to be outnumbering refiners as buyers Friday morning, market players noted. There was speculation that one big Wall Street trader was short, also that the drive up in physical prices might be related to swaps positions.
But there was nothing obvious in the physical market driving prices.

"There have been a lot of secondary buyers, trader types, on the sidelines looking for a bottom to the market. If they are getting nervous and jump in that could get it going," said Hughes of Chevron.

"I'm at a loss for an explanation. But it doesn't matter who is buying. Whether it's Mobil or anybody else, the fact that they're buying is an indication that the market is tight," said one trader in New York.

Indeed, oil industry analysts said gasoline demand so far this summer is at healthy levels flirting with 9.0 million barrels per day. Though production and imports has been ample, any sign of hiccups might be enough to spike prices, traders said.
